description: Squeezing harder is the wrong way to free stiff fingers. The Fist Test measures your tendons' travel, and the right way is glide: many easy trips through the full route. Here is the full-close line, the pulley system, and the daily gliding that gives your hands back.

lines: A fist is a travel report.
beats.title: THE FIST TEST

scenes.narration: The Fist Test, one more time. Open the hand wide, every joint straight, fingers spread. Now close slowly into the tightest fist you own and inspect it like a mechanic. Do the fingertips roll down and press into the base of the palm, all four, evenly? Or does the fist stop early, one finger lagging behind its neighbours like a traveller who missed the train? Measure the gap on the worst finger, in centimetres, and note how the close felt: smooth, or rusty. This episode is about the two ways people respond to that gap. The wrong way squeezes: stress balls, grip trainers, maximal effort against a system whose problem is travel, not strength. The right way glides: many easy trips through the full route, restoring the commute before loading the traveller. By the end you will know which way your hands have been treated. Remember your gap and your stiffest finger. At the end, I grade them.

scenes.label: FINGERTIPS THAT REACH HOME
scenes.narration: The line stands: fingertips pressed fully home is full glide, under two centimetres on the worst finger is short travel, and beyond two is restricted enough to tax every grip you make. Today's addition is the second gauge, the morning clock: how many minutes after waking your hands take to feel like yours. The two numbers tell one story from two angles. The gap measures the route's length. The clock measures the system's irritability. Healing moves both, often the clock first, which makes it the early encouragement this condition rarely offers. Grade yourself at the same time of day, because hands are honest in the morning and flattering by evening, and only compare against your own last score. Methods, including today's, are judged by these two numbers across a month. Nothing else about your hands is a reliable narrator.
scenes.sub: full close: full glide - under 2 cm: short travel - 2+: restricted

beats.text: STRENGTH IS NOT THE MISSING THING

scenes.narration: The wrong way is squeezing, and it is wrong for a mechanical reason worth understanding. Your finger tendons glide through tunnels, held against the bones by pulley guides, and a full fist pulls several centimetres of tendon through that system. When the system is irritated, swollen, or sticky, travel shortens, and the fist stops early. Loading that system maximally, stress balls crushed to failure, grip trainers snapped shut, drags an irritated tendon through its tight tunnels under maximum friction, which is a reliable way to make the tunnels angrier and the travel shorter. The hand feels worked, which everyone mistakes for progress. But strength was never the missing thing. Travel is. A tendon that cannot complete its commute cannot be strengthened through the range it cannot reach, and forcing the issue taxes exactly the structures that need calming. Sequence is the whole therapy: restore the route first, then, and only then, load the traveller.

The right way is gliding, and hand therapists summarised it generations ago: motion is lotion. Every gentle, full-range trip a tendon makes through its tunnel pumps fluid through the system, discourages the sticky adhesions that form between tendon and tunnel wall, and re-teaches the route its full length. The exercises look like nothing: opening wide, hooking the fingers, rolling into a fist, touching each fingertip to the thumb, done slowly, at easy effort, many times a day. Their power is in the arithmetic. A tunnel does not care about your hardest rep; it cares about your total trips, and gliding lets you accumulate hundreds of trips a week at zero recovery cost. Weeks of that arithmetic free a fist the way water frees a rusted hinge, not by force, but by visits. Then, with travel restored, strength work finally has a route to travel on, and grip training becomes the reward instead of the problem.

The right way also sequences the day, because stiff hands live on a schedule. Mornings are the worst act: hours of stillness, cool tunnels, a system that needs warming before it works. So the morning protocol is warmth first, warm water or a warm towel, then glides, then the day's gripping, in that order, every day. Before training, the same sequence in miniature: glides before grips, always, so the first loaded reps travel a route that has already been visited gently. And across the week, gripping work is dosed like everything else in this season: progressed gradually, judged by the next morning's clock. A morning that frees up faster than last week's is the tendon system approving your management in writing. None of this requires talent or equipment. It requires respecting an order of operations, which is the cheapest form of intelligence there is.

Your advantage is frequency, and in this therapy frequency is the entire budget. Gliding costs nothing: no load, no recovery, no soreness tax, so your hands can accumulate trips at a rate no heavy gripper can match. Their hands arrive at every session already owing a day of serious gripping debt; yours arrive comparatively fresh, free to spend the day travelling. Stiffness melts under exactly this pattern, many small trips through the full route, and it melts fastest for the person who can do the most trips without consequence. That is you, by construction. There is a pleasing justice in it: the quality where the strongest hands in the gym have no advantage at all is the quality your hands are built to win. Force was never the currency here. Visits are, and you are rich in visits.
Now glide with me. Open wide, hook the fingers, roll to a fist, open again, slow and full. Forty seconds flowing, twenty to rest, three rounds. Easy effort. Go.

Your week, the right way, in full. Tendon glides morning, noon, and night, a few minutes each, easy effort, full route. Warmth before the morning round, because cold tunnels grade everything harsher. Glides before any gripping work, always, and gripping itself progressed gradually, judged by tomorrow's clock. The stress ball is retired until the fist closes fully; then it returns as strength work, in its proper place at the end of the story. Track both gauges weekly, the gap and the clock, and let them judge the method. And the standing line of this season: a finger that catches, locks, or snaps painfully, swelling that will not settle, stiffness following a fracture or a cut, or a gap that keeps growing, see a professional if it persists. Trigger fingers and stiff joints after injury deserve real assessment, and hands are too important to guess with.

scenes.label: THEN WE MAKE A FIST AGAIN
scenes.narration: So, your grade. Beyond two centimetres means the glide program runs the whole month: trips before strength, warmth before trips, and patience while the route reopens. Under two centimetres is short travel, the grade that responds fastest to frequency; expect the morning clock to improve first and the gap to follow it. A full, smooth close means travel is restored and the story changes: now strength work earns its place, progressed gradually, on a route that can finally carry it. You leave today knowing your hands were never weak. They were under-travelled, which is a scheduling problem, and scheduling problems are the most fixable kind there is. Put your gap in the comments. Just the number. We make a fist again in thirty days.
scenes.sub: 2+ cm: glide program - under 2: trips not force - full close: add strength

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now, same time of day, same slow fist, and we grade that travel again. Subscribe, because next, the season finale: the foot, done right, and the end of the first-step ambush. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Stop Doing finger stiffness Wrong: Train Your finger tendon healing Instead
